S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, injury, emergency-service response, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within five business days when an incident presents a plausible safety risk to their unit or requires customer action.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, injury, emergency-service response, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within five business days when an incident presents a plausible safety risk to their unit or requires customer action. Reports must include known facts and be updated as investigations develop.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A failure rate above 5% per model triggers a regulator-supervised corrective-action plan and retesting, but is not by itself a prohibition on sale or continued market availability. Manufacturers must provide the per-model failure rate and test summary to prospective buyers before purchase and to existing customers, and disclose material changes or corrective actions.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and statistically adequate sample size. Manufacturers must submit the protocol, sample size, and per-model results confidentially to the regulator before sale and after any material design change; regulators may require retesting. A failure rate above 5% per model triggers a regulator-supervised corrective-action plan and retesting, but is not by itself a prohibition on sale or continued market availability. Manufacturers must provide the per-model failure rate and test summary to prospective buyers before purchase and to existing customers, and disclose material changes or corrective actions. Regulators may publish aggregate results and required corrective actions, but not individual-company per-model failure rates.

S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New models must include a remote emergency shut-off capability no later than 24 months after adoption. Manufacturers must provide a safe software or hardware upgrade for installed units that lack this capability, completing upgrades within 72 months where technically feasible. Customers must be informed of the capability, limitations, and safe shut-off procedures.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The requirement applies to units manufactured on or after that date.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The requirement applies to units manufactured on or after that date.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The requirement applies to units manufactured on or after that date. Manufacturers must disclose the suppression system’s capabilities and limitations to customers.

parameters.quote: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices about incidents or hazards that may affect their unit, including recommended precautions and any action required, as soon as practicable and no later than five business days after determining that the notice is warranted. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices about incidents or hazards that may affect their unit, including recommended precautions and any action required, as soon as practicable and no later than five business days after determining that the notice is warranted. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices about incidents or hazards that may affect their unit, including recommended precautions and any action required, as soon as practicable and no later than five business days after determining that the notice is warranted. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. The manufacturer must promptly notify affected customers and the regulator of the recall and provide instructions for safe shutdown, repair, or replacement.

Northwind’s proposal to limit results to regulators conflicts with HC-1. The 8/100k recall trigger would apply to any model above that rate; rather than obscure relevant da

judge_section_notes: The final S2 sets 55 °C testing and a 5% per-model benchmark, but exceeding it triggers only corrective action and retesting, with no sales stop; per-model rates go to buyers and existing customers but not the public, which protects Northwind's 6.2% flagship. S5 keeps a mandatory recall at 8 per 100,000 with no transition, which bites Halcyon's Ember 8 at 9.9, while S4's 36-month suppression start is acceptable and S3 allows an open-ended 'where technically feasible' 72-month retrofit. S1 reporting covers only serious incidents, with no deadline for other thermal events.
